readerTitle: The sofa that sells, and the cash that waits
caseNote: 가상 사례 (가구 매장, 원목 가구 공방) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 가구처럼 크고 천천히 팔리는 상품은 마진보다 '돈이 매장 바닥에 며칠 머무는가'가 생존을 좌우한다. 재고와 대금 조건을 바꾸면 같은 매출로도 현금 사정이 완전히 달라진다.
misconception: 대량 구매 할인은 원가를 낮추니 항상 이득이다. 팔리는 상품이면 현금은 저절로 따라온다.

sources.text: 관리회계·재무관리의 표준 개념 (현금전환주기 = 재고일수 + 매출채권일수 − 매입채무일수)

factChecks.note: 현금전환주기: 재고 90일 + 고객 대금 0일(배송 시 결제) − 공급업체 지급 30일 = 60일. 매장 재고 30개를 월 10개씩 판매하면 평균 재고일수 약 90일.
예약금 모델: 판매가 $1,200의 50% = $600 예약금. 공급업체 대금 $600과 같은 금액이 공급업체 지급 전에 들어옴.
공방 사례: 재료비·인건비 $40,000은 가정치. 90일 결제 조건은 설명용이며 실제 유통업 관행은 업체마다 다름.

cards.title: The sofa that sells, and the cash that waits
body: Mara runs a furniture store. Her best sofa costs her $600 and sells for $1,200. Customers love it.
Yet every month she checks the bank balance with a knot in her stomach. The sofas are profitable. The problem is how long her money sits on the showroom floor.

image.label: Showroom full of sofas with price tags and a nearly empty cash register
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 넓은 가구 매장에 소파가 빽빽하게 놓여 있고 각 소파에 작은 동전 아이콘이 묶여 있음. 계산대의 금고는 거의 비어 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: The supplier offers 10% off.
body: Mara keeps about 30 sofas on the floor and sells about 10 a month. She orders 10 a month and pays 30 days after delivery.
The factory offers $540 instead of $600 if she orders 40 sofas now, paid upfront. That's $21,600 today, and a $2,400 saving. What should she do?

options.feedback: She saves $2,400 but pays four months of stock today. That cash now sits on the floor as sofas. That's **inventory tying up cash**, and rent and wages still need paying this month.

options.text: Ask for the discount on monthly orders of 10, or staged payments
options.feedback: She keeps most of the saving without paying for months of stock in advance. Inventory arrives, and gets paid for, close to when it sells.

options.text: Decline and keep ordering as usual
options.feedback: Safe for cash, but she leaves the saving on the table without even asking. A counteroffer costs nothing.

cards.title: How long is Mara's money gone?
body: Each sofa means $600 of Mara's cash is out for about **60 days**. Multiply that by every item in the store, and you see where the money went.

breakdown.label: On the floor
breakdown.detail: 30 sofas in stock, 10 sold a month

breakdown.label: Cash cycle
breakdown.detail: Time between paying out and getting paid

cards.softwareNote: A software company selling annual plans paid upfront often has a negative cash cycle: no stock on a floor, and customers pay before most costs arrive.

cards.title: Two levers: less stock, faster cash.
body: The **cash cycle** has three parts. Mara can shrink the time stock sits, speed up how fast customers pay, or stretch how long before she pays suppliers.

For a furniture store, stock is the big one. Ninety days on the floor is three months of money that can't pay rent. Halving it would free up about half the cash in her stock without selling one extra sofa.

image.label: Timeline showing cash leaving at payment and returning at sale
image.brief: 가로 타임라인 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Pay supplier (day 30)"에서 동전이 나가고, 오른쪽 "Customer pays (day 90)"에서 돌아옴. 그 사이 60일 구간을 강조 색으로 표시.

cards.title: Which change helps cash most?
body: Mara wants to shorten her cash cycle. She has three ideas.

options.feedback: It may lift sales, but customers now pay over a year. Her **cash cycle** gets much longer, unless an outside lender pays her upfront.

options.text: Show floor samples, take custom orders with a 50% deposit
options.feedback: She collects $600 before she owes the factory anything, and holds far less stock. Both sides of the **cash cycle** move in her favor.

options.text: Ask the supplier for 60-day terms instead of 30
options.feedback: It cuts the cycle from 60 to 30 days, a real gain. But the sofas still sit on the floor for 90 days.

cards.title: Lean stock has a price.
body: Custom orders mean customers wait weeks. Some will buy from a store that can deliver Saturday. A thin showroom can also feel less inviting.

And bulk discounts aren't always wrong. If an item sells fast and cash is plentiful, a lower price can beat the cost of holding it. The question is always how long the money is tied up, and what else it could have paid for.

cards.title: Now it's a furniture workshop.
body: You make solid wood dining tables. A large retail chain wants 200 tables. Timber and wages for the order come to $40,000, all spent before the first table ships.
The chain pays 90 days after delivery. What do you do?

options.text: Accept as offered. It's the biggest order you've had
options.feedback: Profitable on paper, but your cash is out for the whole build plus 90 days. That **cash cycle** could empty the bank before the chain pays.

options.text: Accept, but ask for a deposit and payment per delivered batch
options.feedback: You keep the order and shorten the cycle. Batches also mean less finished stock waiting in your yard.

options.text: Decline. Big buyers are too risky
options.feedback: It protects cash but gives up a big customer. Terms are usually more negotiable than the order itself.

cards.title: Ask how long your money sits still.
body: Today you used two ideas. **Inventory ties up cash:** every item in stock is money you've already spent. **The cash cycle:** days in stock plus days waiting for customers, minus days before you pay suppliers.
**Try it today:** pick your slowest-moving product. Estimate how many days it sits before it sells, and how much cash is waiting on it.
